name: H.H. Holmes

victims.suspected: 9 to 200, most historians estimate fewer than 10 confirmed

victimProfile: Hotel guests, employees, romantic partners, and business associates; primarily women and children
captureMethod: Arrested by Pinkerton detectives in Boston after an insurance fraud investigation led authorities to uncover the murder of his business associate Benjamin Pitezel.
fateDetail: Hanged at Moyamensing Prison in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on May 7, 1896
summary: Born Herman Mudgett, Holmes built a labyrinthine hotel in Chicago during the 1893 World's Fair era, using it to lure and kill victims in what became known as the Murder Castle.
narrative: Herman Webster Mudgett, who adopted the alias H.H. Holmes, is widely regarded as one of the earliest documented serial killers in American history. Born on May 16, 1861, in Gilmanton, New Hampshire, Mudgett grew up in a financially comfortable but reportedly abusive household. He showed early aptitude for science and enrolled at the University of Michigan's medical school, where he graduated in 1884. During his time there, he allegedly began a pattern of insurance fraud involving stolen cadavers that he would disfigure and present as accident victims to collect payouts.

After medical school, Mudgett drifted through several cities under various aliases before arriving in Chicago around 1886. He found work at a pharmacy owned by Elizabeth Holton at the intersection of 63rd and Wallace streets in the Englewood neighborhood. When Holton disappeared under unclear circumstances, Mudgett took over the business. He then began construction on a massive three-story building across the street, which he designed with an intentionally confusing layout. The structure, later dubbed the Murder Castle by journalists, reportedly featured soundproof rooms, hidden passages, sealed vaults, and chutes leading to the basement, where a kiln and vats of acid could be used to dispose of remains.

Holmes timed the building's completion to coincide with the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, which drew millions of visitors to Chicago. He advertised rooms for rent to fairgoers, primarily targeting young women who arrived alone. Employees and romantic partners also fell victim. According to contemporary accounts, Holmes would trap guests in sealed rooms, asphyxiate them with gas lines he had installed, and send their bodies to the basement for disposal. However, historians have cautioned that many of the most lurid details about the Murder Castle originated in sensationalized yellow journalism of the era, and some claims remain unverified.

The exact number of Holmes's victims remains deeply contested. He confessed to 27 murders, though several of those individuals were later found alive. Prosecutors at his trial established evidence for nine killings, while tabloid estimates at the time ranged as high as 200. Most modern historians place the confirmed count significantly lower, noting that many claims were embellished by newspapers competing for readership. The building itself was sold after Holmes's arrest, and it burned under suspicious circumstances before it could be thoroughly examined.

Holmes's downfall began with an insurance fraud scheme involving his associate Benjamin Pitezel. The plan called for Pitezel to fake his own death so Holmes could collect on a life insurance policy. Instead, Holmes killed Pitezel in Philadelphia in September 1894 and collected the payout. He then murdered three of Pitezel's five children as he traveled across the country to avoid detection. Pinkerton detectives, hired by the insurance company, tracked Holmes to Boston, where he was arrested on November 17, 1894.

Charged with the murder of Benjamin Pitezel, Holmes stood trial in Philadelphia in 1895. The jury convicted him after deliberating for less than three hours. He was sentenced to death and, after unsuccessful appeals, was hanged at Moyamensing Prison on May 7, 1896. In the years since, Holmes has become a fixture of American true crime culture, most notably through Erik Larson's bestselling 2003 book The Devil in the White City, which interweaves his story with that of the 1893 World's Fair. The Murder Castle site is now occupied by a United States Post Office building in the Englewood neighborhood of Chicago.

Graduated from the University of Michigan Medical School
Arrived in Chicago and began working at a pharmacy in Englewood under the alias H.H. Holmes
Took over the Englewood pharmacy and began construction of the Murder Castle at 63rd and Wallace streets
Opened the building as a hotel during the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago
Murdered business associate Benjamin Pitezel in Philadelphia as part of an insurance fraud scheme
Arrested by Pinkerton detectives in Boston, Massachusetts
Convicted of the first-degree murder of Benjamin Pitezel in Philadelphia
The Murder Castle burned under suspicious circumstances before a thorough investigation could be completed
Executed by hanging at Moyamensing Prison in Philadelphia

name: Ed Gein

victims.suspected: 2 additional disappearances in the Plainfield area

victimProfile: Middle-aged women from the Plainfield, Wisconsin area who resembled his domineering mother
captureMethod: Arrested after hardware store owner Bernice Worden disappeared; her son, a deputy sheriff, found a sales receipt for antifreeze made out to Gein, leading police to search his farmhouse where Worden's body was found.
sentence: Life imprisonment in a mental institution
fateDetail: Died of respiratory failure linked to cancer at the Mendota Mental Health Institute in Madison, Wisconsin, on July 26, 1984
summary: The Butcher of Plainfield was convicted of two murders and found to have exhumed dozens of corpses. His crimes inspired the characters of Norman Bates, Leatherface, and Buffalo Bill.
narrative: Edward Theodore Gein, known as the Butcher of Plainfield, was a Wisconsin grave robber and murderer whose crimes shocked the nation when they came to light in November 1957. While convicted of only two murders, Gein's case is included here due to its enormous cultural impact and the likelihood that his full criminal history extends beyond the confirmed killings. His crimes directly inspired some of the most iconic figures in horror fiction, including Norman Bates in Psycho, Leatherface in The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, and Buffalo Bill in The Silence of the Lambs.

Gein was born on August 27, 1906, in La Crosse County, Wisconsin. He grew up on a remote farm near the village of Plainfield with his father George, his brother Henry, and his mother Augusta. Augusta Gein was a fanatically religious woman who dominated her sons and taught them that all women outside the family were sinful. George Gein, an alcoholic, died in 1940. Henry Gein died under suspicious circumstances during a brush fire on the family property in 1944; although his death was officially ruled accidental, some investigators later expressed doubt. Augusta herself died of a stroke in December 1945, leaving Edward profoundly isolated.

After his mother's death, Gein sealed off the rooms she had used, preserving them as shrines while he lived in the kitchen and a small adjoining room. He became increasingly reclusive and began making nocturnal visits to local cemeteries, where he exhumed recently buried female corpses. He fashioned items from the remains, including a vest made from a female torso, masks made from facial skin, bowls made from skulls, and lampshades and chair seats covered in human skin. Gein later told investigators that the grave robberies were driven by an obsessive fascination with female anatomy and a desire to construct a suit of female skin that would allow him to become his mother.

Gein's first confirmed murder was that of tavern owner Mary Hogan, who disappeared from her bar in Pine Grove, Wisconsin, on December 8, 1954. Her establishment was found with a trail of blood leading to the parking area, but no body was recovered at the time. His second victim was Bernice Worden, who owned a hardware store in Plainfield. On November 16, 1957, Worden vanished from her shop. Her son Frank, a deputy sheriff, found a sales slip for antifreeze in Gein's name and directed officers to the Gein farmhouse.

What police found at the farm was unprecedented in American criminal history. Worden's decapitated body hung from the ceiling of an outbuilding, dressed out like a deer. Inside the house, officers discovered the heads of both Worden and Hogan, along with remains and artifacts fashioned from an estimated ten to fifteen exhumed bodies. The discovery generated massive national press coverage and permanently altered the landscape of American horror culture.

Gein was arrested on November 16, 1957, and initially found incompetent to stand trial. He was committed to Central State Hospital in Waupun, Wisconsin. In 1968, after more than a decade of treatment, he was declared competent. At trial, he was found not guilty by reason of insanity for the murder of Bernice Worden and returned to institutional care. He was transferred to the Mendota Mental Health Institute in 1978, where he remained a quiet and cooperative patient. Gein died on July 26, 1984, at age 77, from respiratory failure related to cancer. He was buried in Plainfield Cemetery, where his headstone was later stolen and never replaced. Two additional disappearances in the Plainfield area during the 1940s and 1950s were investigated in connection with Gein but never formally resolved.

Murdered hardware store owner Bernice Worden in Plainfield and was arrested the same day after police searched his farmhouse

Found competent to stand trial; tried for the murder of Bernice Worden and found not guilty by reason of insanity
Transferred to Mendota Mental Health Institute in Madison, Wisconsin
Died at age 77 at Mendota Mental Health Institute from respiratory failure linked to cancer

name: Herb Baumeister

victims.suspected: At least 11 to 25, based on bone fragments recovered from Fox Hollow Farm

victimProfile: Young men from the Indianapolis gay bar scene, typically in their 20s and 30s, of similar age and build
captureMethod: Never apprehended. After his wife granted police permission to search Fox Hollow Farm in June 1996 and bone fragments were discovered, Baumeister fled to Canada and died by suicide before he could be arrested.
sentence: None; died before charges were filed
fateDetail: Shot himself at Pinery Provincial Park in Ontario, Canada, on July 3, 1996
summary: Indianapolis businessman who buried the remains of at least 11 men on his 18-acre Fox Hollow Farm estate. He killed himself in Canada in 1996 as investigators closed in.
narrative: Herbert Richard Baumeister was an Indianapolis-area businessman who is believed to have murdered at least eleven men during the 1980s and 1990s, burying their remains on his eighteen-acre estate known as Fox Hollow Farm in Westfield, Indiana. Because Baumeister died by suicide before he could be arrested or charged, he was never tried, and the full scope of his crimes remains unknown. The case is one of the most significant unsolved serial murder investigations in Indiana history.

Baumeister was born on April 7, 1947, in the Butler-Tarkington neighborhood of Indianapolis. He reportedly displayed troubling behavior from a young age and spent time receiving psychiatric treatment as a young adult. Despite these warning signs, he married Juliana Saiter in 1971, and the couple raised three children. In 1988, using a loan from his mother, Baumeister and his wife opened the first of several Sav-A-Lot thrift stores in the Indianapolis area. The business was successful enough to fund the family's move to Fox Hollow Farm, a former horse estate in Hamilton County, in 1991.

Beginning in the early 1990s, investigators with the Indianapolis Police Department and the Marion County Sheriff's Department noticed a pattern of disappearances among young men from the city's gay bar district along East Washington Street. The missing men were of similar age, height, and weight. Witnesses described a well-dressed man who frequented the bars using the alias Brian Smart. One survivor of an encounter with the man provided a partial description and a license plate number, which investigators eventually traced to Baumeister.

The first physical evidence surfaced on the Baumeister property in 1994 or 1995, when his teenage son discovered a human skull in the wooded area behind the house. Baumeister dismissed it as an old anatomical skeleton that had belonged to his physician father. His wife, who was growing increasingly concerned about his erratic behavior, did not report the find to police at that time. It was not until 1996, as the Baumeisters' marriage deteriorated and Julie began cooperating with investigators, that she granted permission for a search of the property.

On June 24, 1996, detectives and forensic anthropologists began excavating the wooded acreage behind the main house. What they found was staggering. Over the following weeks, investigators recovered more than ten thousand bone fragments, representing the partial remains of at least eleven individuals. Many of the bones had been burned, crushed, or otherwise processed, making identification extremely difficult. Forensic analysis determined that the victims had been strangled. Investigators believe Baumeister killed the men while his wife and children were away on vacations or trips, then disposed of the remains on the property.

As the investigation accelerated, Baumeister fled the state. He drove to Ontario, Canada, and on July 3, 1996, shot himself at Pinery Provincial Park. He left a three-page suicide note that addressed his failing business and marriage but made no mention of the killings. Because he died before charges could be filed, there was no trial, and the criminal investigation effectively ended. Authorities in Hamilton, Marion, Hancock, and Shelby counties considered Baumeister a suspect in additional disappearances along the Interstate 70 corridor between Indiana and Ohio during the 1980s, though no formal charges were ever brought in those cases.

Efforts to identify the Fox Hollow Farm remains continued for decades. In 2022, Hamilton County Coroner Jeff Jellison relaunched the identification effort using advanced DNA technology. By 2024, the remains of Manuel Resendez, who disappeared in 1993, and Allen Livingston, also missing since 1993, had been positively identified. The total number of presumed victims has risen to at least thirteen, though investigators believe the actual count could be as high as twenty-five. The case remains an active investigation.

Died by self-inflicted gunshot wound at Pinery Provincial Park in Ontario, Canada
Hamilton County Coroner Jeff Jellison relaunched victim identification efforts using advanced DNA analysis
Remains of Manuel Resendez and Allen Livingston positively identified, raising the confirmed victim count to 13

name: Belle Gunness
aliases: The Black Widow of La Porte

victims.suspected: 14 to 40 or more, including suitors, husbands, and children

victimProfile: Wealthy male suitors recruited through matrimonial newspaper advertisements, as well as husbands and some children
captureMethod: Never apprehended. Her crimes were discovered after her La Porte farmhouse burned on April 28, 1908, and investigators unearthed the remains of numerous victims on the property. Whether Gunness died in the fire or staged her death remains unresolved.
fateDetail: A headless body found in the fire ruins was initially identified as Gunness, but her death was never confirmed. Numerous reported sightings occurred for decades afterward.
summary: Norwegian-born Black Widow who lured men to her La Porte, Indiana farm through personal ads, killed them for their money, and may have faked her own death in a 1908 fire.
narrative: Belle Gunness, born Brynhild Paulsdatter Stoerseth on November 11, 1859, in Selbu, Norway, is one of the most prolific female serial killers in American history. Over a period spanning roughly two decades, she is believed to have murdered as many as forty people, primarily wealthy male suitors whom she lured to her farm in La Porte, Indiana, through matrimonial advertisements in Norwegian-language newspapers. Her story combines elements of insurance fraud, romantic deception, and mass murder, and her ultimate fate remains one of the great unsolved mysteries of American criminal history.

Gunness emigrated from Norway to the United States in 1881, settling in Chicago where she joined a growing Scandinavian immigrant community. In 1884, she married Mads Ditlev Anton Sorenson. The couple operated a confectionery store that burned under suspicious circumstances, yielding an insurance payout. Their subsequent home also suffered a fire. Mads Sorenson died in 1900 under circumstances that the family doctor attributed to heart failure, though another physician suspected strychnine poisoning. Gunness collected life insurance proceeds estimated at over eight thousand dollars.

With her insurance money, Gunness purchased a farm outside La Porte, Indiana, in 1901. She married Peter Gunness in April 1902. Within eight months, Peter was dead, reportedly killed when a heavy sausage grinder fell from a shelf and struck his head. The coroner noted inconsistencies, and a coroner's jury investigated but ultimately did not bring charges. Belle collected another insurance payout of approximately thirty-five hundred dollars from her second husband's estate.

Now a widow with a profitable farm, Gunness began placing advertisements in Scandinavian newspapers across the Midwest, seeking prosperous men interested in marriage. The ads typically requested that suitors bring cash or assets to demonstrate their seriousness. A succession of men traveled to La Porte to court her. Among the documented visitors were Ole B. Budsberg, who was last seen at a La Porte bank in April 1907, and Andrew Helgelien, a South Dakota farmer who arrived in January 1908 carrying his life savings of nearly three thousand dollars. None of these men were seen again after arriving at the farm.

In early 1908, Gunness fired her farmhand Ray Lamphere and publicly accused him of threatening to burn her house down. She visited a lawyer to draft a will and expressed fears for her safety. In the early morning hours of April 28, 1908, the Gunness farmhouse was destroyed by fire. In the ruins, authorities found the bodies of Gunness's three children, Myrtle, Lucy, and Philip, as well as a headless adult female body initially identified as Belle. The absence of the head raised immediate suspicions.

Further investigation of the property revealed a horror. Investigators unearthed the dismembered remains of at least ten men and two women from garbage-filled pits behind the house. The victims had been poisoned, bludgeoned, or dismembered and buried in quicklime. Some remains could not be identified. The scope of the discovery prompted a national sensation, and La Porte was overrun by journalists and curiosity seekers.

Ray Lamphere was arrested and charged with arson and murder. At his trial in November 1908, he was convicted of arson but acquitted of murder. Before his death from tuberculosis in December 1909, Lamphere reportedly told a fellow prisoner that Gunness had staged the fire, placed a substitute body in the ruins, and fled with her accumulated fortune. Whether Gunness actually died in the 1908 fire has never been conclusively determined. Reported sightings continued for decades, and a 2008 forensic examination of exhumed remains raised additional questions without providing definitive answers. Her case remains officially open.

Ole B. Budsberg, a documented suitor, was last seen at a La Porte bank

name: John Norman Collins
victimProfile: Young women and teenage girls, predominantly college students in the Ann Arbor-Ypsilanti area
captureMethod: Arrested after witness testimony placed his last victim, Karen Sue Beineman, on his motorcycle shortly before her disappearance. Hair clippings found on her body were forensically linked to the basement of a house belonging to Collins's uncle, where Collins had been house-sitting.
sentence: Life imprisonment without the possibility of parole
fateDetail: Serving life without parole in a Michigan state prison; has maintained his innocence
summary: Eastern Michigan University student convicted of one of seven murders of young women in the Ann Arbor-Ypsilanti area between 1967 and 1969. Police attributed all seven killings to him.
narrative: John Norman Collins, known as the Ypsilanti Ripper, was an Eastern Michigan University student convicted in 1970 for the murder of Karen Sue Beineman, one of seven young women killed in the Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti area of southeastern Michigan between 1967 and 1969. Although formally convicted of only one murder, Collins was identified by investigators as the prime suspect in all seven killings, which terrorized the university communities and became collectively known as the Michigan Murders.

Collins was born on June 17, 1947, in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, and grew up in the Detroit metropolitan area. By most outward appearances, he was unremarkable. He was described as handsome and athletic, a former high school baseball star who enrolled at Eastern Michigan University to study elementary education. He was a member of a fraternity and maintained a sociable public persona. Beneath this surface, however, police would later allege that Collins was systematically targeting young women in the area.

The series of murders began on July 9, 1967, when nineteen-year-old Mary Fleszar, an EMU student, disappeared while walking near campus. Her badly decomposed body was found approximately a month later on an abandoned farm in Superior Township. Over the next two years, six more young women were murdered in the area. Joan Schell, a University of Michigan student, was found on July 5, 1968. Jane Mixer, a University of Michigan law student, was found on March 21, 1969. Maralynn Skelton, only sixteen years old, was discovered on March 25, 1969. Dawn Basom, thirteen, was found on April 16, 1969. Alice Kalom, a University of Michigan graduate student, was discovered on June 8, 1969. The victims had been subjected to varying methods of violence, including strangulation, stabbing, and bludgeoning.

The final victim in the series was Karen Sue Beineman, an eighteen-year-old EMU freshman from Grand Rapids, Michigan. On July 23, 1969, Beineman was seen leaving a wig shop on a motorcycle with a young man she had just met. The shop owner later identified Collins as the rider. Beineman's body was found three days later in a ravine near the Huron River. A critical piece of forensic evidence emerged: hair clippings found on Beineman's body were identified as coming from the basement of a house belonging to Collins's uncle, a Michigan State Police officer. Collins had been house-sitting at the property during his uncle's vacation at the time of the murder.

Collins was arrested on July 31, 1969. His trial for the murder of Karen Sue Beineman began on July 20, 1970, in Ann Arbor. The prosecution's case rested heavily on the wig shop eyewitness identification and the forensic hair evidence linking the crime to the uncle's basement. On August 19, 1970, a jury found Collins guilty of first-degree murder. He was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

Collins was never formally charged in any of the other six Michigan murders, though investigators publicly stated they considered him the prime suspect. A Monterey County, California, grand jury indicted Collins in April 1970 for the murder of Roxie Ann Phillips, a teenager killed in that state, but the charge was not pursued after his Michigan conviction. Collins has maintained his innocence throughout his imprisonment and continues to serve his sentence in a Michigan state prison. The case was chronicled in Edward Keyes's 1976 book The Michigan Murders, which remains the most comprehensive account of the investigation.

name: Coral Eugene Watts
victimProfile: Women and girls of various ages and racial backgrounds, attacked seemingly at random; Watts did not sexually assault his victims
captureMethod: Arrested in Houston, Texas, after attempting to drown a woman in her apartment bathtub. Her roommate escaped through a second-floor window and screamed for help, drawing police to the scene while Watts was still inside.
sentence: Two consecutive sentences of life without parole
fateDetail: Died of prostate cancer on September 21, 2007, at a Michigan prison in Jackson
summary: The Sunday Morning Slasher terrorized Michigan and Texas through the 1970s and 1980s. He confessed to 13 murders but is suspected of killing 80 to 100 women across multiple states.
narrative: Carl Eugene Watts, known as Coral and nicknamed the Sunday Morning Slasher, was a serial killer who operated primarily in Michigan and Texas during the 1970s and early 1980s. Unlike many serial killers, Watts did not sexually assault his victims and appeared to derive no obvious gratification beyond the act of killing itself. His case is also notable for a controversial plea bargain that nearly allowed him to walk free despite being suspected of dozens of murders.

Watts was born on November 7, 1953, in Killeen, Texas. His parents divorced when he was two years old, and his mother moved with her children to Inkster, a suburb of Detroit, Michigan, where she worked as a high school art teacher. As a child, Watts survived a severe case of meningitis, which some medical professionals speculated may have caused developmental effects. He was reported to have tortured and killed animals as a youth and received psychiatric treatment during his teenage years, including a diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder.

Watts's first known attacks occurred in Michigan in the mid-1970s. His confirmed killing history begins around 1974, when he was approximately twenty years old. His method of victim selection was unusual in that it appeared almost entirely random. He targeted women and girls of various ages and racial backgrounds, with no consistent pattern that investigators could identify. The attacks were characterized by sudden, extreme violence, often involving stabbing, strangulation, drowning, or bludgeoning. Many occurred in the early morning hours, giving rise to his nickname.

By 1979, Watts had escalated significantly. On October 31, 1979, he stabbed thirty-five-year-old Jeanne Clyne to death as she walked home from a doctor's appointment on a sidewalk in the affluent Detroit suburb of Grosse Pointe Farms. In late 1980, an Ann Arbor police sergeant observed a man in a brown Pontiac Grand Prix stalking a female pedestrian and recorded the license plate, which traced back to Watts. An intensive surveillance operation followed, but investigators lacked sufficient evidence for an arrest. Watts relocated to the Houston, Texas, area in March 1981, and the attacks continued there.

Watts's downfall came on May 23, 1982, in Houston. He forced his way into an apartment where two young women were present. After killing one woman by drowning her in her bathtub, he attempted to do the same to twenty-year-old Lori Lister. Her roommate, Melinda Aguilar, managed to escape through a second-story window and screamed for help, alerting neighbors and police. Officers arrived while Watts was still in the apartment and arrested him.

What followed was one of the most controversial plea bargains in Texas legal history. With limited direct evidence linking Watts to other murders and facing the possibility that he might be acquitted, prosecutors in Harris County offered him a deal: in exchange for confessing to thirteen murders and providing information about his victims, Watts would plead guilty to a reduced charge of burglary with intent to commit murder and receive a sixty-year sentence. Under Texas sentencing guidelines at the time, this meant Watts could have been eligible for release as early as 2006.

The prospect of Watts's release galvanized law enforcement across multiple states. Through the persistent efforts of investigators and victims' family members, new evidence was developed linking Watts to the 1979 murder of Helen Dutcher in Michigan and the earlier killing of Gloria Steele. In 2004, Watts was tried and convicted in Michigan for these murders, receiving two consecutive sentences of life without parole. He died of prostate cancer on September 21, 2007, at a Michigan prison facility in Jackson. Detectives believe his actual victim count may be between eighty and one hundred or more, which would make him one of the most prolific serial killers in American history.

Relocated from Michigan to the Houston, Texas area; attacks continued in Texas
Arrested in Houston after a surviving victim's roommate escaped and alerted police during an attack
Accepted plea bargain in Harris County, Texas; confessed to 13 murders and received 60-year sentence for burglary with intent to commit murder

Died of prostate cancer at age 53 in a Michigan prison facility in Jackson

name: Samuel Little

victims.suspected: 60 confirmed by FBI out of 93 confessions; believed all 93 are credible

victimProfile: Predominantly marginalized women, including sex workers, women struggling with addiction, and women of color whose deaths were often ruled overdoses or attributed to undetermined causes
captureMethod: Arrested at a homeless shelter in Louisville, Kentucky, on a narcotics warrant and extradited to California, where DNA evidence linked him to three unsolved Los Angeles murders from the late 1980s.
sentence: Multiple life sentences without parole in California, Texas, and Ohio
fateDetail: Found dead in his prison cell in Los Angeles County, California, on December 30, 2020, at age 80
summary: The most prolific serial killer in United States history according to the FBI. Little confessed to 93 murders spanning 35 years and at least 19 states; the FBI has confirmed 60 of those confessions.
narrative: Samuel Little, born Samuel McDowell on June 7, 1940, in Reynolds, Georgia, is recognized by the Federal Bureau of Investigation as the most prolific serial killer in United States history. Over a criminal career spanning approximately thirty-five years, Little confessed to ninety-three murders committed between 1970 and 2005 across at least nineteen states. The FBI's Violent Criminal Apprehension Program has confirmed at least sixty of those confessions, a number that exceeds the verified victim counts of Gary Ridgway, Ted Bundy, and John Wayne Gacy.

Little was raised primarily by his grandmother in Lorain, Ohio, after his mother, who he said was a teenage prostitute, largely abandoned him. He dropped out of school and began accumulating a lengthy criminal record in the 1950s, with arrests for shoplifting, fraud, assault, armed robbery, and solicitation across multiple states. Over the following decades, he was arrested more than one hundred times in twenty-four states. He served approximately ten years in prison on various charges and twice escaped murder convictions before his crimes were finally connected.

Little's victims were predominantly marginalized women, including sex workers, women struggling with addiction, and women of color. He targeted people whose disappearances or deaths were unlikely to draw significant investigative attention. Many of his victims' deaths were originally classified as overdoses, accidents, or undetermined causes. His preferred method was manual strangulation, which often left few traces that a medical examiner could definitively attribute to homicide, particularly in cases where the victim had preexisting health conditions or a history of substance use.

The breakthrough in the case came in September 2012, when Little was arrested at a homeless shelter in Louisville, Kentucky, on a drug warrant. He was extradited to California, where Los Angeles Police Department detectives had linked his DNA to three cold case murders from 1987 to 1989. The victims were Carol Alford, Guadalupe Apodaca, and Audrey Nelson. In September 2014, a jury found Little guilty of three counts of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to three consecutive life terms without the possibility of parole.

The scope of Little's crimes remained largely unknown until 2018, when Texas Ranger James Holland gained Little's trust during a series of extended interviews. Little then began confessing to murders across the country in extraordinary detail. He described each victim's appearance, the location of the killing, and the circumstances with remarkable specificity. He also produced colored pencil drawings of many of his victims from memory, which the FBI released publicly to assist in identification efforts. His confessions ultimately totaled ninety-three separate killings.

FBI crime analysts assessed Little's confessions as credible across the board, noting his consistent accuracy about verifiable details such as locations, dates, and victim descriptions. By October 2019, the Bureau had confirmed at least sixty of the ninety-three confessions, and investigations into the remaining cases continued. Little was additionally convicted of murders in Texas and Ohio, bringing his total convictions to at least eight across three states.

Samuel Little died on December 30, 2020, at the age of eighty, in a prison cell in Los Angeles County, California. His case exposed significant failures in how law enforcement agencies across the country tracked and investigated the deaths of marginalized women over several decades. The FBI's ViCAP team credited the case with demonstrating the critical need for improved national coordination in linking unsolved homicides across jurisdictional boundaries.
